1.pericope_label: And Solomon made affinity with Pharaoh king of Egypt, and took Pharaoh’s daughter, and brought her into the city of David, until he had made an end of building his own house, and the house of the Lord, and the wall of Jerusalem round about. Only the people sacrificed in high places, because there was no house built unto the name of the Lord, until those days. And Solomon loved the Lord, walking in the statutes of David his father: only he sacrificed and burnt incense in high places. And the king went to Gibeon to sacrifice there; for that was the great high place: a thousand burnt offerings did Solomon offer upon that altar.

schools.summary: Ellicott finds no fault in the marriage, observing that the sacred historian finds none either, that the Egyptians were never regarded with the aversion felt towards the Canaanite races, and that the match is nowhere connected with the later declension, so that the queen may literally have forgotten her own people and her father's house; he supplies the political setting from Egypt's own records, a weak and divided Tanite dynasty with Assyrian power in corresponding abeyance, and does the chapter's most careful work on the high places, distinguishing sacrifice to false gods from unauthorised sanctuaries of the Lord and setting out the objects the prohibition served.

Gill asks why no Egyptian ruler is named in Scripture between Moses and this point though the kingdom was powerful and near, answers from Diodorus Siculus that the kings of that stretch had nothing worthy of relation, canvasses Vaphres and Sesostris as candidates with the reported letters about temple workmen, and locates the high-place worship concretely on house tops and hills and particularly at Gibeon, four or five miles from Jerusalem, where the tabernacle then stood.

Clarke treats the Egyptian marriage as a plain breach of express law, granting that it strengthened the kingdom as the alliance with Tyre did but asking whether politics should prevail over the command forbidding Israel to give daughters to or take daughters from such nations; he holds that in this alliance were sown the seeds of the apostasy in which Solomon so long lived and so awfully died, and answers the apologists point by point, denying any evidence that the bride was a proselyte, refusing to let the Song's place in the canon settle anything, and producing Nehemiah and the later chapter on the strange women as express reproof.

debates: Whether the Egyptian marriage was sinful, where Clarke holds it a direct breach of express law and the seed of the later apostasy, and Ellicott holds that neither the historian nor the narrative of the declension finds any fault in it.

What the apologists' case for the marriage is worth, Clarke setting out four grounds, that the bride was a proselyte, that God was not displeased, that the Song could not stand in the canon with an idolatrous spouse, and that Solomon is nowhere blamed, and rejecting each.

What the high places were and why they were later forbidden, where Ellicott distinguishes two kinds and finds the prohibition aimed at local corruption, at visible forms, and at a breach of national unity, while Gill simply reports the practice as it stood.
outliers: Ellicott reads the prohibition of unauthorised sanctuaries as a remarkable spiritual education for the worship of an invisible God without local emblems, preparatory to the perfect spirituality of the future.
Gill reports a heathen writer who names the Pharaoh Vaphres and claims that letters between him and Solomon about workmen for the temple were still preserved.

5.pericope_label: In Gibeon the Lord appeared to Solomon in a dream by night: and God said, Ask what I shall give thee. And Solomon said, Thou hast shewed unto thy servant David my father great mercy, according as he walked before thee in truth, and in righteousness, and in uprightness of heart with thee; and thou hast kept for him this great kindness, that thou hast given him a son to sit on his throne, as it is this day. And now, O Lord my God, thou hast made thy servant king instead of David my father: and I am but a little child: I know not how to go out or come in. And thy servant is in the midst of thy people which thou hast chosen, a great people, that cannot be numbered nor counted for multitude. Give therefore thy servant an understanding heart to judge thy people, that I may discern between good and bad: for who is able to judge this thy so great a people? And the speech pleased the Lord, that Solomon had asked this thing. And God said unto him, Because thou hast asked this thing, and hast not asked for thyself long life; neither hast asked riches for thyself, nor hast asked the life of thine enemies; but hast asked for thyself understanding to discern judgment; Behold, I have done according to thy words: lo, I have given thee a wise and an understanding heart; so that there was none like thee before thee, neither after thee shall any arise like unto thee. And I have also given thee that which thou hast not asked, both riches, and honour: so that there shall not be any among the kings like unto thee all thy days. And if thou wilt walk in my ways, to keep my statutes and my commandments, as thy father David did walk, then I will lengthen thy days. And Solomon awoke; and, behold, it was a dream. And he came to Jerusalem, and stood before the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and offered up burnt offerings, and offered peace offerings, and made a feast to all his servants.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the dream institutionally rather than as a favour, contrasting direct communication of this kind with David's indirect knowledge of God's will through Nathan and Gad and through the priest and taking it for perhaps the first sign of an abeyance of the prophetic office and a loss of leadership in the priesthood, and adding that the vision by dream is of a lower type than the waking vision; he defines the gift as the wisdom of the ruler, notes that Solomon looks for it as an inspiration rather than a fruit of experience, and holds that only length of days was conditional and that alone was not fulfilled.

Gill maximises the supernatural in the dream, making it no common natural dream but a prophetic night vision of the sort God used with his prophets, in which Solomon kept the full use of his reasoning powers and the Lord really did appear by some display of his glory; he reads the request as political wisdom for ruling Israel well rather than spiritual or natural understanding, explains that it pleased God because Solomon had respect to the people's good and God's honour rather than his own advantage, and keeps to what the waking showed, that Solomon knew the dream true at once by finding himself possessed of a wisdom he had never had.

Clarke naturalises the dream and then deflates his own naturalising, noting that it came the night after the sacrifices and probably after earnest prayer, so that the images occupying the mind by day recurred at night, but concluding that we need not carry the matter so far into miracle, since God might be author of the extraordinary wisdom as he was of the riches; he reads the request as the true science of government, glosses the not knowing how to go out or come in as an infant learning to walk, and presses the hardest question in the chapter, whether Solomon ever received all this wisdom at all, finding no character in the sacred writings more disappointing.

debates: What kind of dream this was, where Gill makes it a prophetic night vision with a real display of the divine glory, Clarke allows that it may have followed the day's prayer by ordinary means, and Ellicott reads it as a lower mode of revelation and a symptom of prophetic abeyance.

How much of the promise was kept, where Ellicott holds that only length of days was conditional and that one point failed, the rest receiving an extraordinary fulfilment, while Clarke asks whether the whole was conditional and whether Solomon ever received the wisdom at all.

What the wisdom asked for was, Gill making it political rather than spiritual or natural, Clarke the true science of government, and Ellicott the ruler's discernment to do true justice between man and man.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the vision by dream is mostly recorded of men outside the covenant, of the early stages of revelation, and of the lapse of the prophetic succession during the captivity.

Clarke holds it as credible that Solomon lay down ignorant and rose wiser than all the children of men as that he lay down with a scanty revenue and woke to find his treasury full, yet adds that the seeds of understanding did not continue to grow.
Ellicott dates the reign at forty years and judges that Solomon's age could hardly have exceeded sixty, against Josephus, who stretches the reign to eighty.

16.pericope_label: Then came there two women, that were harlots, unto the king, and stood before him. And the one woman said, O my lord, I and this woman dwell in one house; and I was delivered of a child with her in the house. And it came to pass the third day after that I was delivered, that this woman was delivered also: and we were together; there was no stranger with us in the house, save we two in the house. And this woman’s child died in the night; because she overlaid it. And she arose at midnight, and took my son from beside me, while thine handmaid slept, and laid it in her bosom, and laid her dead child in my bosom. And when I rose in the morning to give my child suck, behold, it was dead: but when I had considered it in the morning, behold, it was not my son, which I did bear. And the other woman said, Nay; but the living is my son, and the dead is thy son. And this said, No; but the dead is thy son, and the living is my son. Thus they spake before the king. Then said the king, The one saith, This is my son that liveth, and thy son is the dead: and the other saith, Nay; but thy son is the dead, and my son is the living. And the king said, Bring me a sword. And they brought a sword before the king. And the king said, Divide the living child in two, and give half to the one, and half to the other. Then spake the woman whose the living child was unto the king, for her bowels yearned upon her son, and she said, O my lord, give her the living child, and in no wise slay it. But the other said, Let it be neither mine nor thine, but divide it. Then the king answered and said, Give her the living child, and in no wise slay it: she is the mother thereof. And all Israel heard of the judgment which the king had judged; and they feared the king: for they saw that the wisdom of God was in him, to do judgment.

schools.summary: Ellicott calls the judgment an instance of intuitive sagacity, cutting the knot of a hopeless difficulty by an appeal to maternal instinct which might have failed but was the only one possible, and locates the wisdom precisely in knowing how to risk failure rather than be reduced to impotence and how to go straight to the heart of a difficulty when the slow regular approaches of science are impossible, which is where men recognise a touch of genius and where Scripture here recognises the wisdom of God.

Gill weighs the character of the two women both ways and comes out the other side from Clarke, reporting the Targum's victuallers or innkeepers and the argument that common prostitutes do not usually bear children or care for them as these plainly did, but setting against it that no husbands are mentioned, that they live together in one house and alone, and that they are impudent and brawling and litigious, which gives great suspicion that the received reading is the true one; he also supplies the motive the text leaves out, the mother who had overlaid her own child resorting to the stratagem through fear of punishment for such negligence or because of the disgrace of it.

Clarke rejects the English rendering of the two women outright, preferring the Chaldee, which he calls the best judge in the case, and its tavern-keepers, on three grounds, that harlots would hardly have dared appear before Solomon, that common women would not likely have had children, and that such persons would not have been permitted under the previous reign; he denies the judgment was miraculous, calling it a proof of sound judgment, penetration and acquaintance with human nature but surely not of extraordinary and supernatural wisdom, supports the deflation with the parallel of Ariopharnes and the arrow, and is scrupulous enough to say that he reports that story on Grotius's authority and has not himself found the place in Diodorus.

debates: What the two women were, where Clarke rejects the received rendering on the Chaldee's authority and three further reasons, and Gill, after giving the argument on the other side, finds the evidence of the narrative itself pointing back to the received reading.

Whether the judgment was miraculous, which both Ellicott and Clarke deny, Ellicott making it intuitive sagacity and a touch of genius and Clarke sound judgment and acquaintance with human nature expressly not produced as proof of supernatural wisdom.
What became of the losing woman, which Clarke raises and leaves unanswered, observing that we are not told though justice certainly required that she be punished for her lies and her fraud.
outliers: Clarke explains the absence of any husband by supposing the women away about their necessary occupations, the case being too urgent to wait.

Clarke brings in the heathen parallel of Ariopharnes, who settled which of three claimants was the dead king's son by commanding each to shoot an arrow into the body, and notes that it works by the same covert appeal to affection as the judgment here.

Clarke reads the people's fear as the measure of the decision, since it proved to them that they could not impose upon the king and that he was taught of God, judged impartially and could not be deceived.
